id: Man's Short Life and Foolish Ambition

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

O man, O man, what high ambition growsWithin his brain, and yet how low he goes!To be contented only with a sound,Wherein is neither peace nor life nor body found.

Keywords: How, With, Saw

outputs.L1:
In gardens sweet, I marked each flower,  
How it did spring, and bud, and bloom, then wither and die.  
And, contemplating man’s short stay,  
I saw that man, like those flowers, passes away.  

Yet he builds houses, thick and strong and high,  
As though he were to live to all eternity.  
He hoards a mass of wealth, yet cannot fill  
His empty mind; still he covets more.  

To gain or keep, such falsehood will he use;  
Wrong, right, or truth—no base means will he refuse.  
I would not blame him, could he keep death away,  
Or ease his pains, or make his sleep secure;  

Or buy Heaven’s mansions, become as the gods,  
And with his gold rule the stars, the moon, and the sun;  
Command the winds to blow, the seas to obey,  
Level their waves, and bid their breezes stay.  

But he has no power, except to die,  
And care in life is only misery.  
This care is but a word, an empty sound,  
Wherein no soul nor substance can be found;  

Yet, as his heir, he makes it inherit,  
And all he has he leaves unto this spirit.  
To gain this child of Fame, this bare word,  
He fears no danger, neither fire nor sword.  

All horrid pains and death he will endure,  
Or anything, if only fame he may procure.  
O man, O man, what lofty ambition grows  
Within his brain—and yet how low he goes!  

To be contented only with a sound,  
Wherein neither peace, nor life, nor body can be found.
outputs.L2:
As I observed the lovely flowers in the garden, I noticed how each one emerged, formed a bud, opened into bloom, then faded and died. Thinking on this, I saw that human life passes in the same brief way.

Yet people build houses that are solid, crowded, lofty, and strong, as though they expected to remain alive forever. They gather great piles of riches, but their restless minds are never satisfied; they continue to desire more. To gain wealth or preserve it, they will resort to deceit, and they will not reject any shameful method, whether it violates justice, honesty, or truth.

I would not condemn such behavior if money could keep death away, lessen suffering, guarantee peaceful sleep, purchase heavenly dwellings, make a person divine, or allow gold to command the stars, moon, and sun. Nor would I blame it if wealth could order the winds to blow, force the seas to submit, flatten their waves, or stop their breezes.

But human beings possess no such power, except the power to die; and the anxieties of life bring only misery. This “care” they serve is nothing more than a word, a hollow noise, without soul or real substance. Even so, they treat it like an heir, leaving everything they own to this empty spirit.

For the sake of that child called Fame—nothing more than a bare name—they will face every danger, including fire and sword. They will suffer terrible pain and even death, or anything else, if only they can obtain renown.

O humanity, how lofty are the ambitions that grow in the mind, and yet how low people sink: they are satisfied with nothing but a sound, a thing that contains no peace, no life, and no body.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the sight of flowers blooming and withering, and sees in them a clear image of human life. Flowers appear in beauty for a short time, flourish briefly, and then fade away. In the same way, human beings live only for a limited span. However bright, strong, or prosperous a life may seem, it is still fragile and temporary. The natural cycle of growth and decay reminds the speaker that all living things are subject to time.

Yet human beings often behave as if they could live forever. They build strong houses, gather possessions, and store up wealth, as though these things could protect them from the limits of life. Instead of accepting the shortness of human existence, people try to surround themselves with signs of permanence and security. Their houses, treasures, and material comforts give them the illusion that they have power over time and death.

The speaker also criticizes the pursuit of wealth. Wealth may provide comfort, but it cannot truly satisfy the mind or bring lasting peace. The desire for riches often grows stronger the more it is fed, leaving people restless and discontented. In seeking wealth, people may be tempted into dishonesty, falsehood, and wrongdoing. What begins as a desire for security can become a source of moral corruption.

Human power, the speaker suggests, is far more limited than people like to believe. No amount of wealth can prevent death, remove all suffering, or give human beings control over nature. Riches cannot stop the body from aging, cannot protect anyone completely from grief, and cannot command the winds, seasons, or forces of the world. In the face of mortality and nature’s power, human possessions are shown to be weak and uncertain.

The speaker also turns to the pursuit of fame. People are willing to endure danger, hardship, and pain in order to win a name for themselves. They may risk their lives, sacrifice their peace, or abandon what is truly valuable simply to be praised by others. But fame itself is described as empty and insubstantial. It is only a sound, a name spoken by other people, without any lasting or real substance.

Overall, the speaker presents a meditation on the vanity of human ambitions. Life is brief, like the life of a flower, yet people chase wealth, power, and fame as if these could give them permanence. In the end, such pursuits cannot overcome death or provide true fulfillment. The speaker encourages a recognition of human limits and a deeper awareness of what is genuinely meaningful.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a meditation on human mortality and the fragile nature of earthly life. It compares human beings to flowers, which bloom for a short time, display their beauty, and then inevitably fade and wither. Through this image, the poem emphasizes that life is temporary, no matter how strong, beautiful, successful, or admired a person may appear. Just as flowers cannot resist the passing of the seasons, human beings cannot escape aging, decline, and death.

After establishing this sense of life’s brevity, the poem turns to a criticism of human ambition. People spend their limited time chasing wealth, power, fame, and social status, believing these things will bring security or happiness. However, the poem suggests that such pursuits are misguided because they cannot change the basic condition of human existence. Riches can be lost, power can disappear, and fame can fade just as quickly as physical beauty. None of these achievements can prevent death, nor can they provide lasting peace.

The poem therefore presents worldly ambition as empty and deceptive. It shows that human beings often devote themselves to possessions and reputation while ignoring the fact that life is short and uncertain. In the end, everyone must face the same fate, regardless of rank or success. By comparing people to flowers and exposing the limits of wealth and fame, the poem encourages readers to recognize the vanity of earthly striving and to reflect on what, if anything, can give life deeper meaning beyond temporary achievements.
outputs.L5:
**How I Saw the World With New Eyes**

How we look at the world can change everything. Sometimes, the same place, the same people, and the same daily routines can feel completely different when we choose to see them with a fresh perspective.

One morning, I walked through a quiet park and saw the sunlight shining through the trees. I had passed that park many times before, but this time I noticed the small details: the birds singing, the leaves moving gently in the wind, and people smiling as they walked by. With a calm mind, even ordinary things seemed beautiful.

That moment taught me how important it is to slow down and pay attention. With patience and curiosity, we can saw—or rather, see—the beauty hidden in everyday life. Sometimes, happiness is not found in big events, but in the simple things we often overlook.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a 17th-century metaphysical poet about human mortality, greed, ambition, and the emptiness of fame, using flowers in a garden as the opening image.
counterfactuals.output:
In beds of state the morning tulips stand,  
Each cup a little kingdom in the sun;  
The rose holds court, the lily lifts her hand,  
And all their painted policies are spun  
From dew, that bribing pearl, which night bestows  
To buy one hour’s favor from the rose.

See how the marigold, with golden eye,  
Counts up the light, as usurers count their gain;  
Yet when the west shuts down the bankrupt sky,  
Her minted face is folded up again.  
So man, that yellow flower of dust and breath,  
Lends out his soul at interest to death.

Ambition is a vine: it climbs, it clings,  
It courts the wall, it flatters every stone;  
It would be neighbour to the nests of kings,  
And make the borrowed battlement its own.  
But frost, that pale corrector of desire,  
Writes “Nothing” on its green, aspiring fire.

The greedy bee, with thigh of treasure proud,  
Robs every blossom for a drop of sweet;  
Yet honeyed thefts, though murmured of aloud,  
Cannot preserve the robber from defeat.  
His little empire hums, and then is gone—  
A sound entombed in silence before dawn.

What is our fame? A scent upon the air,  
A rumor roses breathe and winds betray;  
A name cut deep in marble’s stony care,  
Which rain reads out, and lichens eat away.  
The laurel, too, that crowns the victor’s brow,  
Was once a leaf, and is a leafless bough.

O flesh, proud flower, why dost thou thus contend,  
To purchase shadows with thy certain hours?  
Thy root is in the grave; there all things end—  
The schemes of merchants and the dreams of powers.  
For death, God’s gardener, with impartial knife,  
Prunes back the overgrowth we christen life.

Then let me bloom not wide, but inward still,  
No gaudy banner for the noon to praise;  
Let not my sap be spent in climbing will,  
Nor all my spring consumed in seeking bays.  
One humble seed of grace, beneath the sod,  
Outlives the gardens of the great with God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an early modern English moral poem that begins with contemplating flowers blooming and dying, then reflects on man's short life, wealth-hoarding, falsehood, and futile pursuit of fame.
counterfactuals.output:
Behold the flow’rs, how freshly they arise,  
With painted cheeks to court the morning skies;  
The lily pale, the rose of crimson hue,  
Drink up the sun, and sip the silver dew.  
Yet ere the day hath drawn his golden wain,  
Their pride is bow’d, their beauty turn’d to pain;  
The stalk that stood so brave at prime of light  
Lies low, and withers in the arms of night.  

Such is man’s life: a blossom and a breath,  
New-born to-day, to-morrow ripe for death.  
His cradle standeth hard beside his grave;  
He comes as one that nothing here may have,  
And yet he builds, as though the earth were sure,  
And lays up treasure, counting dust secure.  

O wretched he, that heaps his shining store,  
And, having much, still hungers after more;  
That locks his gold from widow, friend, and poor,  
Yet cannot bar pale Death from out his door.  
His chests are full, his conscience lean and thin;  
He gaineth land, and loseth peace within.  

Some clothe their tongues in fair and silken lies,  
And make deceit a ladder where to rise;  
But truth, though poor, shall stand when craft is gone,  
As stars abide when painted fires are done.  
The fox may prosper for a little space,  
Yet shame at last shall overtake his pace.  

And what is fame, that men pursue with cries,  
But wind that passeth through a thousand skies?  
A name in brass, a rumor, and a sound,  
A fading garland on a fading mound.  
The trump of praise grows hoarse, the laurel sear;  
Time writes, then wipes, the glory men hold dear.  

Then mark the flow’rs, that preach without a tongue:  
Be humble, mortal, whilst thy days are young.  
Do good, love truth, let mercy be thy gain;  
For wealth is smoke, and worldly pomp is vain.  
So shalt thou fade, when God shall bid thee cease,  
Not into darkness only, but to peace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a rhymed philosophical poem about how people build houses and gather riches as if they will live forever, even though death makes ambition meaningless.
counterfactuals.output:
They raise their walls against the sky,  
And carve their names in stone,  
As if the years would pass them by,  
And leave their flesh alone.  

They count their coins with careful breath,  
And lock their gardens tight,  
Yet every vault belongs to death,  
And every roof to night.  

They plant their flags on borrowed ground,  
They call the dust their own,  
But time will make without a sound  
A ruin of the throne.  

For what is gold beneath the clay?  
What mansion keeps the bone?  
The hand that grasps is swept away,  
The heart departs alone.  

So build, but know the beams will fall;  
So earn, but do not cling.  
The grave is waiting under all—  
A silent, leveling king.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that sounds like Margaret Cavendish or Anne Bradstreet, meditating on flowers, mortality, covetousness, worldly care, and the vanity of human fame.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon a Bed of Flowers**

When I beheld the garden in her pride,  
Her silken troops in painted ranks appear,  
The tulip brave, the rose with blushes dyed,  
The violet low, yet sweet unto the ear;  
Methought each leaf did whisper as it grew,  
“Poor flesh, behold thy glass, and read thee true.”

For in the morn they lift their heads full high,  
As courtiers do that newly come to grace;  
At noon they spread their little bravery,  
And drink the sun with an aspiring face;  
But ere the night hath drawn her sable wing,  
Their crowns lie dust, their beauties take no wing.

O man, that for a fading garland strives,  
And sells his peace to purchase empty breath,  
Who heaps up earth, as if earth kept our lives,  
And builds against the battery of death;  
Consider lilies, how they neither care,  
Yet wear more glory than thy labours wear.

The covetous hand would grasp the meadow’s store,  
And call each blossom by the name of “mine”;  
It counts its gold, then hungers after more,  
And makes a god of what was digged from mine.  
Yet can that gold, when pulse and colour fly,  
Buy one poor daisy from mortality?

Worldly care, like canker in the bud,  
Eats out the sweetness of our small delight;  
We toil, we fret, we trouble flesh and blood,  
Then sleep beneath the field we plagued by right.  
The rose is wiser, who, her hour being done,  
Falls without murmur, having kissed the sun.

And what is fame, that painted butterfly,  
Which men pursue through briars, mire, and thorn?  
A sound, a shade, a plume tossed up on high,  
A breath begot at eve and dead at morn.  
The greatest names, though graven deep in stone,  
Are read by dust, when all their praise is gone.

Then let me learn from flowers humility,  
To bloom not proudly, nor to fear decay;  
To scent the air with quiet charity,  
And give, not hoard, my little life away.  
For he that lays his treasure in the skies  
Shall find, when flowers fall, a crown that never dies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a classical-style devotional/memento mori poem condemning man's obsession with wealth and reputation, ending with the idea that fame is only an empty sound.
counterfactuals.output:
O man, why heap thy glittering dust,  
And call the moth’s inheritance thine?  
Why build on breath, repose on rust,  
And crown thy brow with fading vine?

The merchant counts his shining store,  
The lord his acres, towers, and name;  
Yet Death stands waiting at the door,  
And all their reckonings end the same.

The marble speaks; the banners fall;  
The feast is cold, the music fled;  
The worm keeps court in kingly hall,  
And crowns are level with the dead.

What boots the praise of mortal tongues,  
The painted honor men bestow?  
A passing bell for all their songs,  
A little dust, a little woe.

Seek Him whose treasure cannot fade,  
Whose mercy outlives tomb and stone;  
For all that pride and gold have made  
Is gone when God is left alone.

So lay thy vain ambitions down,  
Let humble prayer thy heart surround;  
For wealth is clay, and power a frown,  
And fame is but an empty sound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
